questions.q: What I/O pattern does a data file typically see?
options: Random I/O — pages read and written wherever the relevant data happens to live
Purely sequential I/O, identical to the log file
No I/O at all until a backup runs
Only write I/O, never reads
questions.explain: Data files see random I/O because queries and checkpoints touch pages scattered throughout the file, unlike the log's strictly ordered writes.

questions.q: Why does the log file see sequential I/O?
options: Write-ahead logging writes every change to the log first, in strict order, before the data page is written
The log file is read far more often than it's written
SQL Server compresses the log file automatically
The log file only stores index rebuild operations
questions.explain: Write-ahead logging guarantees durability by logging a change before the corresponding data page changes, and as long as nothing competes for the disk, this produces one continuous sequential write stream.

questions.q: Why should data files and log files sit on separate physical disks?
options: The data file's random I/O interrupts the log's sequential stream if they share a disk, and separation also protects tail-log backup capability if the data disk fails
SQL Server refuses to start if they're on the same disk
It only matters for tempdb, not user databases
It has no real effect; it's purely a legacy recommendation
questions.explain: Sharing a disk breaks up the log's sequential writes with the data file's random seeks, slowing every commit; separate disks also mean a data-disk failure doesn't take out the log, enabling a tail-log backup.

options: A Virtual Log File — a physically contiguous internal chunk that makes up the transaction log
A type of data file extension
A view in sys.databases
A backup file format
questions.explain: The log file is internally divided into VLFs; SQL Server grows the log by adding VLFs and reuses them once their contents are no longer needed.

questions.q: What causes VLF fragmentation, and why does it matter?
options: Many small, repeated autogrowth events create a huge number of small VLFs, which slows crash recovery and database restarts
It's caused by AUTO_SHRINK on the data file and has no effect on the log
It happens only when PAGE_VERIFY is set to NONE
It is unrelated to log file growth settings
questions.explain: A log file that grew through many small autogrowth increments ends up with many small VLFs, and SQL Server must process every VLF during recovery — sizing the log correctly upfront avoids this.
